graph_apply.title: Apply a batch of changes
graph_apply.description: Create, patch or delete stored records (entities) and their named groups of fields (components) in one atomic transaction: either every change is accepted or none is. `change` is an array of bundles, where a bundle is one entity’s components as one JSON object: {entity: {eid}, <component>: {<columns>}}, the same shape a client’s apply() takes. An omitted column is left unchanged, a null column is cleared, a null component is removed, and $delete: true deletes the entity. An eid is an entity’s unique string id. Generate the eid yourself, or write '$name' as the eid and read the eid the graph assigned from the result. Where this store keeps names, alias: {name: '<your name>'} beside a '$name' eid makes the write idempotent: writing the same name again patches the entity that already has it instead of creating a second one, and a name can be used wherever an eid can. A read-modify-write can state what it was based on: $was: {doc: {body: "<hash>"}}, for example, gives, per component and column, the SHA-256 of the value you read (null for “it had none”), and the whole batch is refused, naming the column and its current value, if that value has changed since. That is compare-and-set: two callers spending the same balance or claiming the same reward, and only one of them succeeds. The result is the transaction as applied, one bundle per entity: {entity: {eid, num}}, every component as written, the stamps the graph added (created, updated), and the '$alias' you named it by. Every entity that was deleted, including any deleted as a consequence, is returned as {entity, tombstone: {}} and nothing else. This tool’s input schema is the store’s vocabulary (schema): every component, column (field) and type; graph_schema reports the same thing at length. The schema is open: a component or column declared after you connected still reaches the graph, and a column nobody declared is refused by the server. check: true is a dry run: every check is made and the whole transaction is then rolled back, so the result is a report with JSON in content.body describing what would have been written, with every '$name' resolved to the eid it would get, or the refusal, worded exactly as it would be for a kept write. That is how a plan of several entities and the relationships (edges) between them is proven before any of it is written. Documentation: https://yaks.app/docs/store.

change.description: bundles to apply together: each needs entity: {eid} and the component fields to write; omitted fields stay unchanged

check.description: true to validate without keeping the proposed changes and return a JSON report of the result; default false

graph_query.title: Query entities
graph_query.description: Find stored records (entities) by filtering on their named groups of fields (components) and fields (columns). Returns whole bundles: JSON objects with entity: {eid} and all the record’s component objects. A query string selects them: '.task.status=open&.filed.priority<3'. It is made of filters written as .component.column=value (or .column=value when unambiguous), joined with &, with lists (a,b), ranges (1..9), != for not equal, ~= for text containing a value, < or > comparisons, '.prop!' for present and '.prop=' for absent. Directives go in the same string: .order=, .limit=, and .refs=<id> for everything that references an entity. filters, if passed, are joined onto q with &. Documentation: https://yaks.app/docs/querying.

q.description: query filters, e.g. .task.status=open&.filed.priority<3; use graph_schema to discover valid components and columns

filters.description: extra dot-params, joined onto q with &

limit.description: return at most this many entities

graph_show.title: Show entities
graph_show.description: Read one or more stored records (entities) by their unique string id (eid), each returned whole: every component it has, plus every entity that references it, each as its own bundle in {bundles}: a JSON object with entity: {eid} and named groups of fields (components). Relationships stored as edge entities are returned in that same format. This is lookup by identity, not search: pass eids, or the names entities are addressed by where this store keeps names (an eid wins over a name spelled the same way). Set backrefs to false to get only the entities themselves.

ids.description: the eids or names of the entities to read

backrefs.description: also return the entities that reference them (default: true)

graph_schema.title: Read the schema
graph_schema.description: Read this store’s vocabulary (schema): each component is a named group of fields attached to an entity, a stored record; its columns are those fields. Returns JSON in content.body at one of three levels of detail. With no arguments: the index, every component with a one-line meaning and its column names. With component (one name or several): that component in full, each column’s type and meaning, which columns are server-owned or unique, what references it and what it references, and an example bundle that writes it. With kind: the definition of a display category such as task, plus summaries of the components it is displayed with. If both kind and component are passed, kind selects the answer. Read the index first, then ask for the component you are about to write. Documentation: https://yaks.app/docs/components.

component.description: a component to read in full, or a list of them

kind.description: a display category declared by the schema, such as task; returns its definition and associated components

search.title: Search text
search.description: Full-text search over this store’s entities: the ones whose text matches, ranked best first, as bundles: JSON objects containing each record’s id and named groups of fields. Searches the text fields this server indexes. Use graph_query when you know which columns you are filtering on, and this when you only know what the text says. Documentation: https://yaks.app/docs/querying.

limit.description: return at most this many entities
